name: Ananias (Ananias, husband of Sapphira, who sold a property and withheld part of the proceeds)
title: The man who lied to the Holy Spirit
summary: Ananias was a believer in the early church in Jerusalem, where Christians shared their possessions with one another out of free will. He and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of property, but secretly kept back part of the proceeds while pretending to give everything. When Ananias laid the money at the apostles' feet, Peter exposed the deception through insight from the Holy Spirit. Peter clarified that the property and the money had always been under Ananias's control – the sin lay in lying to God, not in keeping something for himself. Immediately after the confrontation, Ananias fell down dead, and three hours later Sapphira met the same fate when she upheld the same lie. The event left deep awe throughout the entire community of faith and stands as a startling testimony to God's holiness and to the profound connection between truth and fellowship in the people of the new covenant.

keyEvents.title: Sale of property and withholding of money
keyEvents.description: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a property they owned but secretly agreed to keep back part of the sale price. Ananias brought the rest of the money and laid it at the apostles' feet as if it were the full amount.

keyEvents.title: Peter confronts Ananias
keyEvents.description: The apostle Peter, guided by the Holy Spirit, saw through the deception and confronted Ananias directly. He pointed out that the property and the money had always been under Ananias' own control, but that by lying he had lied not to people but to God himself.

keyEvents.title: Ananias' sudden death
keyEvents.description: When Ananias heard Peter's words, he fell down and died. Some young men came, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him. Great fear seized all who heard what had happened.

keyEvents.title: Sapphira's death
keyEvents.description: About three hours later Sapphira came in, unaware of what had happened to her husband. When Peter asked her about the sale price, she repeated the lie. Peter then said that the feet of those who had buried her husband were already at the door. She fell down immediately and died, and the young men carried her out and buried her beside her husband.

keyEvents.title: Fear throughout the whole church
keyEvents.description: The incident with Ananias and Sapphira brought deep reverence to the entire church and to all who heard about it. It highlighted the holiness of the new community of faith and the seriousness of living honestly before God.

versions.summary: Ananias was a member of the early Christian church in Jerusalem. He and his wife Sapphira sold a property but withheld part of the proceeds while pretending to give the full amount to the apostles. When Peter confronted him with the lie, Ananias fell down dead, and his story became a warning example of deception toward God and the church.
versions.title: The man who lied to the Holy Spirit
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'disciple' is acceptable, but it can be debated whether Ananias should be called a 'disciple' in the traditional sense. He was a member of the early church, but his role is primarily known as a warning example. It may be more precise to add 'member of the Jerusalem church' as a role.; [minor] The second key element ('Ananias brings the money to the apostles') largely overlaps with the first ('Sale of property'), since both refer to Acts 5:2. These could usefully be combined to avoid repetition.; [major] Footnotes are missing. The profile should include footnotes covering historical, theological, or linguistic aspects of the story of Ananias and Sapphira.; [minor] The summary is good, but it could usefully mention that Sapphira also died shortly after, to give a more complete picture of the event.

versions.summary: Ananias was a member of the early Christian church in Jerusalem. He and his wife Sapphira sold a property but withheld part of the proceeds while pretending to give the full amount to the apostles. When the apostle Peter, led by the Holy Spirit, confronted him with the deception, Ananias fell down dead. About three hours later, Sapphira repeated the lie and also died. The incident became a warning example of deception toward God and created great reverence throughout the entire church.
versions.title: The man who lied to the Holy Spirit
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is almost identical to version 1 (which received a score of 7). It begins with exactly the same sentence: 'Ananias was a member of the early Christian church in Jerusalem. He and his wife Sapphira sold ...' Since there is an earlier version, the text should be rephrased to provide a fresher and more distinct presentation.; [minor] The role 'property owner' could be added, since Ananias is explicitly described as someone who owned and sold property. This gives a more complete role profile.; [minor] In the event 'Sapphira's death', it states that Peter told her that those who had buried her husband 'were standing at the door and would carry her out too'. The Bible text says that Peter said 'the feet of those who buried your husband are at the door', as a statement rather than a threat. The wording could be nuanced slightly.

versions.summary: Ananias belonged to the first Christian congregation in Jerusalem, where believers voluntarily shared their resources. Together with his wife Sapphira, he sold a property, but secretly withheld part of the sale price. When Ananias brought the remainder of the money to the apostles' feet and presented it as the full amount, the apostle Peter – guided by the Holy Spirit – exposed the deception. Peter emphasized that the sin was not in keeping some of the money, but in lying to God. Ananias fell dead immediately, and shortly afterward the same judgment struck Sapphira, who repeated the lie. This dramatic event sent shockwaves through the church and served as a powerful reminder of God's holiness and the seriousness of living truthfully before him and the community.
versions.title: The man who lied to the Holy Spirit
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is well written and theologically precise, but it structurally resembles the two previous versions, both of which began by describing Ananias as a member of the church. The current version varies the opening slightly with 'belonged to the first Christian assembly', but could benefit from further differentiation to avoid repetition. Nevertheless, the wording is sufficiently distinct and content-rich.; [minor] The role 'property owner' is correct according to the text, but it could also have been relevant to include something like 'deceiver' or 'warning example' to capture the biblical function his role plays in the narrative. This is, however, a stylistic consideration.; [minor] The footnotes are very good and cover linguistic, theological, and archaeological aspects. The archaeological footnote is somewhat general and could benefit from being more specific, but it is not incorrect.

footnotes.text: The name Ananias (Greek: Ἁνανίας) is the Greek form of the Hebrew Hananiah (חֲנַנְיָה), which means 'YHWH has been gracious.' It is a remarkable irony that a man with a name testifying to God's grace became the object of God's immediate judgment.

The early Christian church in Jerusalem practiced voluntary communal sharing where believers sold properties and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–37). Ananias' sin was not in keeping part of the money, but in lying about it. Peter emphasizes in Acts 5:4 that the property and the money were always his to dispose of freely.

The story of Ananias and Sapphira has clear parallels to Achan's sin in Joshua 7, where dishonesty with consecrated items led to judgment on the sinner. Both events occur at the beginning of a new era in God's people's history—the conquest of Canaan and the rise of the early church—and both serve as warning examples of the seriousness of standing honestly before God.

Several scholars have interpreted this event as an expression of 'sacred law' or direct divine judgment in the apostolic church, where the community's holiness was maintained through divine intervention. Parallels are found in the Old Testament, including Nadab and Abihu offering strange fire (Lev 10:1–3) and Uzzah's death at the ark of the covenant (2 Sam 6:6–7).

Archaeological findings from Jerusalem in the first century AD confirm that property transactions were common and that land holdings in the areas around the city had significant value. Ossuaries, inscriptions, and other finds from this period provide insight into the rich cultural and economic environment in which the early Christian church operated.

The Greek verb νοσφίζω (nosfizō), used in Acts 5:2 regarding Ananias' action, is the same verb used in the Septuagint (LXX) for Achan's embezzlement in Josh 7:1. Luke's word choice thus suggests a deliberate literary parallel between the two events.

Rabbinic tradition places great emphasis on the prohibition against lying (cf. Lev 19:11). In the Talmud (Sanhedrin 92a), the seriousness of lying is discussed, and several rabbis stress that whoever lies is like one who denies God's presence. The Ananias episode can be read in light of this Jewish ethical tradition in which the early Christian church was rooted.
